items.title: Day 1 Overview
items.body:
Day 1 · Unit 1: Whole Numbers

Day 1 Overview

How our number system works, how to read and write large numbers, and how to round for quick estimates — the building blocks everything else in this course builds on.

Learning Objectives Covered Today

  • Identify place value
  • Read and write whole numbers
  • Round whole numbers

Why It Matters

This unit builds the foundational math skills needed for entry-level office and business work — reading a number correctly, writing it down without dropping a zero, and rounding for a quick estimate come up constantly in business math: reading inventory counts, writing dollar amounts, and estimating totals before you check the exact number.

Today’s Tasks

  1. Place Value — read, then complete Practice 1
  2. Reading and Writing Whole Numbers — read, then complete Practice 2
  3. Rounding Whole Numbers — read, then complete Practice 3
Note

Practice 1-3 are self-check practice quizzes, not graded — use them to see what's solid and what needs another look before Day 2, when we start adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing whole numbers.

items.title: Place Value — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 7 · CBO Objective: Identify place value

Place Value

Whole numbers are made up of the digits 0 through 9. Every digit has a place value — how much it’s worth — based on where it sits in the number.

Breaking It Down

Think of place value like money in your wallet: a $1 bill and a $100 bill both show the digit “1”, but their position (which bill they're printed on) makes them worth completely different amounts. Numbers work the same way — the digit 3 is worth 3, 30, 300, or 3,000,000 depending purely on which column it sits in.

Example 1: Find the Value of a Digit

What is the value of the 5 in 85,406?

Ten Th.ThousandsHundredsTensOnes
85406
Step 1
Find the digit: 5
Step 2
Read the column: thousands
Step 3
5 × 1,000 = 5,000

Example 2: A Bigger Number

What is the value of the 7 in 2,573,940?

MillionsHun. Th.Ten Th.ThousandsHundredsTensOnes
2573940
Step 1
Find the digit: 7
Step 2
Read the column: ten thousands
Step 3
7 × 10,000 = 70,000
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Mixing up place and value is the #1 mix-up here: if asked for the value of the 5 in 85,406, the answer is 5,000 — not just “5” and not “thousands.” The place is the position's name (thousands); the value is what the digit is actually worth there (5,000). Also remember place values increase as you move right to left, not left to right.

Video: Math Antics - Place Value (Math Antics, YouTube)

items.title: Reading and Writing Whole Numbers — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 8-9 · CBO Objective: Read and write whole numbers

Reading and Writing Whole Numbers

Commas split a whole number into groups of three digits, counting from the right. Reading left to right, you say each group's digits followed by its group name — million, thousand — except the last group, which has no name.

Breaking It Down

A big number is really just several 3-digit numbers stacked together, each one given a group name as you move left: thousand, million, billion. Work one comma group at a time — read (or write) its three digits, say its name, then move to the next group.

Example 1: Read a Number Aloud

How do you read 2,043,000?

Millions,Thousands,Ones
2043000
Step 1
Group by 3, from the right: 2 | 043 | 000
Step 2
Name each group — the last group (000) is silent
Step 3
Read it: two million, forty-three thousand

Example 2: Write a Number from Words

Write “three million, four hundred eight thousand, six hundred” as a whole number.

Millions,Thousands,Ones
3408600

Highlighted digits are places the words didn’t mention — hold them with a zero.

Step 1
Split the words into groups: three | four hundred eight | six hundred
Step 2
Fill each group to 3 digits, holding empty spots with 0
Step 3
Combine with commas: 3,408,600
Common Mistakes to Avoid

When writing a number FROM words, it's easy to drop a zero-holding place by accident — e.g. writing 3,48,600 instead of 3,408,600. After you write each group, count the digits: every group except possibly the very first must have exactly three digits. Also double-check comma placement lines up with your groups, not with wherever feels natural.

Want a video for this one?

This skill is really place value applied to bigger numbers — if you want a refresher, revisit the Place Value video on the previous page, or check the Khan Academy link on the Want More Practice? page at the end of today.

items.title: Rounding Whole Numbers — Reading
items.body:
Day 1 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 10-11 · CBO Objective: Round whole numbers

Rounding Whole Numbers

Cory’s car weighs 2,374 pounds. What is the weight of her car to the nearest 100 pounds? To answer that, you round off 2,374 — rounding makes a number easier to use when you don’t need the exact value.

Breaking It Down

Rounding answers one question: what’s the closest, simpler number I could use instead? A manager quoting “about $2,400” instead of “$2,374.18” is rounding on purpose. The whole rule comes down to checking exactly one digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you’re rounding to.

Example 1: Round to the Nearest Hundred

Round 2,374 to the nearest hundred.

ThousandsHundredsTensOnes
Before2374
After2400
Step 1
Locate the target place: hundreds (3)
Step 2
Check the next digit: 7 — that's 5 or more, so round up
Step 3
3 + 1 = 4, zero out the rest: 2,400

Example 2: Rounding That Carries Over

Round 29,624 to the nearest thousand.

Ten Th.ThousandsHundredsTensOnes
Before29624
After30000
Step 1
Locate the target place: thousands (9)
Step 2
Check the next digit: 6 — round up
Step 3
9 + 1 = 10, so it carries: 2 becomes 3. Zero out the rest: 30,000
Common Mistakes to Avoid

Only look at one digit — the one right after your target. Students sometimes glance at two or three digits and second-guess themselves; ignore everything except that single next digit. Also remember every digit to the right of your target becomes a zero, even if some of them were already going to “round down” on their own.

Video: Math Antics - Rounding (Math Antics, YouTube)
